source: Krishnamurthy et al. (2024) Can large language models explore in-context?
finding: Of all LLM and prompt setups tested as bandit agents, only GPT-4 with a hint to explore, per-arm summary statistics and chain of thought explored well.
numbers: MAB, 5 arms, gap 0.2, T=100, N=10 or 20 replicates. Gpt-4 had 72 configs, 10 per main run; Gpt-3.5 48 configs, N=20 (about 200K queries). GPT-4 basic prompt: suffix failure in >60% of replicates (T=500, N=20).
quote: only one configuration resulted in satisfactory exploratory behavior
limits: Small N and short T. Only one bandit family. Models are June 2023 versions.
agent_relevance: Raw history in the prompt is not enough. An agent loop that must pick between attempts needs an external tally, not a transcript.

source: Krishnamurthy et al. (2024) Can large language models explore in-context? (failure modes)
finding: Two failure modes: suffix failure (best arm never chosen again after early rounds) and uniform-like failure (all arms sampled near-equally, no narrowing).
numbers: Of 10 main Gpt-4 configs, three avoid suffix failure; two of these show uniform-like failure (high MinFrac). Only BSSC0 (summarized history, reinforced CoT, temperature 0) succeeds. Greedy baseline has the same suffix-failure signature.
limits: Suffix-failure statistic is a surrogate; total reward hides it at T=100 because of lucky bimodal replicates.
agent_relevance: Check an agent for greedy lock-in on its first good-looking idea, and for flat spreading of budget across all ideas. Both are measurable.

source: Krishnamurthy et al. (2024) Can large language models explore in-context? (small models)
finding: Gpt-3.5 did worse than Gpt-4 in every setting. Llama2-13B (4-bit) was worse still, with suffix failure rates from Greedy level upward.
numbers: Llama2: hard MAB only, 32 configs, N=10. Gpt-3.5: N=20 across 48 configs.
limits: Quantised small model; generalising to current open models is unproven.
agent_relevance: Exploration is a capability that rises with model size. A weak solver cannot be made to allocate well by prompt alone.

source: Krishnamurthy et al. (2024) Can large language models explore in-context? (summarisation ablation)
finding: The same winning prompt without external summarisation fails. Chain of thought alone on raw history did not rescue exploration.
numbers: Same CoT and hint, raw history vs per-arm counts and means: failure vs success (Gpt-4, hard instance).
limits: Summarising is easy in bandits; the authors say it is a hard design problem in richer settings.
agent_relevance: G12 should be implemented as code outside the model: keep per-option counts and success rates, show them to the model, let it decide.

source: Nie et al. (2024/2025) EVOLvE: Evaluating and Optimizing LLMs For Exploration (BanditBench)
finding: Benchmark of 16 MAB and 2 contextual-bandit tasks in natural language. Inference-time help from a classical algorithm raised exploration for large models. Fine-tuning on UCB traces helped most.
numbers: Pairwise win-rate (%), MAB, columns Gemma-2B, Gemma-9B, Flash, Pro. Raw History: 7.6, 10.5, 27.7, 45.5. Summarized History: 10.5, 5.3, 34.8, 60.0. Algorithm-Guided (UCB stats in prompt): 4.9, 4.1, 32.2, 59.6. UCB itself 90.6. 30 runs per setup; T=1000 for K=30, T=200 for K=10.
limits: Win-rate metric uses t-tests; Gemini 1.5 era models. Full MAB suite cost about $15.9K for Flash. Table parsed from PDF text, column order inferred.
agent_relevance: The best prompt-only scaffold gets Pro to about 60 against UCB at about 91. A gap remains; offload the allocation rule to code.

source: Nie et al. (2024/2025) EVOLvE: Evaluating and Optimizing LLMs For Exploration (BanditBench) (contextual bandit)
finding: In contextual bandits, raw history is near useless; algorithm-guided support helps a lot.
numbers: CB win-rate: Flash RH 0.0, Pro RH 7.1; Flash AG 46.4, Pro AG 64.3; LinUCB 96.4.
limits: Only 2 CB tasks; table parsed from PDF text.
agent_relevance: When options are described by features, an explicit scoring rule in the prompt beats free reading of history.

source: Nie et al. (2024/2025) EVOLvE: Evaluating and Optimizing LLMs For Exploration (BanditBench) (fine-tuning and few-shot)
finding: Fine-tuning on oracle UCB trajectories lifted Flash above Pro. Few-shot demonstrations helped Flash but hurt Pro.
numbers: MAB win-rate: Flash oracle fine-tune 65.6 (trained on hard) vs 54.5 (trained on easy); Flash few-shot with easy demos 50.2 vs hard demos 43.0. Few-shot hurt Pro in MAB and CB.
limits: Authors suspect hand-written few-shot examples disrupt CoT in big models; not tested directly.
agent_relevance: Few-shot examples can lower a strong reasoner. Training is outside our scope (no weight changes).

source: Nie et al. (2024/2025) EVOLvE: Evaluating and Optimizing LLMs For Exploration (BanditBench) (regret scaling)
finding: Fits regret curves by model and support. Weak models stay in linear regret. Large models with algorithm help come close to sublinear.
numbers: Gemma-2B and 9B remain linear regret; Pro with AG or SH near sublinear; fine-tuned Flash sublinear with lower slope. Explore fraction under SH: Flash falls 11.3% to 1.1% over steps; Pro 79.0% to 10.5%; Gemma-9B rises 6.9% to 16.5%.
limits: Descriptive fits, not theorems.
agent_relevance: Small models explore too little or too randomly; a harness should fix an exploration floor for weak solvers.

source: Binz & Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 (davinci) beat humans on a two-armed bandit (horizon task) on total regret but showed no directed exploration.
numbers: Horizon task: GPT-3 mean regret 2.72 (SD 5.98) vs humans 3.24 (SD 10.26), t(38878)=-5.03, p<.001. Short horizon: no difference from humans (p=.97). No horizon-by-information interaction, so no directed exploration; only traces of random exploration.
limits: GPT-3 (2022), text-only prompt, no reasoning chain.
agent_relevance: Good average reward can hide the lack of information-seeking. Test for it directly: does the agent try the least-tried option when it has a long budget left?

source: Binz & Schulz (2023) (decisions from descriptions)
finding: On over 13,000 gamble problems, only the largest GPT-3 beat chance and it did not reach human level; it showed 3 of 6 Kahneman-Tversky biases (framing, certainty, overweighting small probabilities).
numbers: 13,000+ problems from the Peterson et al. data set; Davinci above chance t(29134)=-16.85, below human t(29134)=-11.50.
limits: Single model family of that date.
agent_relevance: Value estimates from described options are noisy in LLMs; keep numeric tallies outside the model.

source: Coda-Forno et al. (2023) Meta-in-context learning in large language models
finding: GPT-3 on a two-armed bandit got better across successive tasks inside one context (meta-in-context learning) and matched Greedy after four tasks, still slightly behind UCB.
numbers: 500 simulations. In-context regression beta=-0.221 (SE 0.012), t=-35.8. Prior mean reward fell from M=545.22 (SD 6359) before to M=6.49 (SD 4.41) after, close to the true generator.
limits: GPT-3 only, simple bandit, 2 arms.
agent_relevance: Prior calibration matters: an agent can learn how hard problems are from a few earlier solved ones in the same run.

source: Schubert et al. (2024) In-context learning agents are asymmetric belief updaters
finding: LLMs in two-option learning tasks learn more from better-than-expected outcomes (optimism). The bias flips when the outcome of the unchosen option is shown and vanishes when someone else is said to sample.
numbers: Three instrumental learning tasks adapted from cognitive psychology; Meta-RL agents show similar patterns. Human data from Lefebvre et al. 2017 compared. No effect sizes recorded.
limits: Effect size varies by task; not all models tested.
agent_relevance: Framing of who chose the option changes how the model weighs wins. Report results to the model with neutral wording, and show outcomes of options not taken.

source: Pan, Xie & Wilson (2025) Large Language Models Think Too Fast To Explore Effectively
finding: In an open-ended exploration game (Little Alchemy 2), most LLMs found fewer elements than humans in 500 trials; reasoning models did better. Standard LLMs rely on uncertainty, humans mix uncertainty and empowerment.
numbers: Elements found in 500 trials: LLaMA3.1-8B 9, LLaMA3.1-70B 25, GPT-4o 35, DeepSeek-R1 85, o1 177, humans 42 (29,493 humans, 4,691,033 trials). o1 vs humans t=9.71, p<0.001; R1 t=3.40; GPT-4o t=-5.48; 70B t=-6.39; 8B t=-28.12.
limits: One game; the long-chain models are different families so size and reasoning are mixed.
agent_relevance: Reasoning models explore much better in open settings. Use thinking-mode models for the allocation judge.

source: Pan, Xie & Wilson (2025) Large Language Models Think Too Fast To Explore Effectively (mechanism)
finding: Sparse autoencoder probing: uncertainty and choice are encoded in early blocks, empowerment later, so non-reasoning LLMs commit before the value signal is ready.
numbers: Higher temperature gave a small gain (beta=0.124, z=5.06, p<0.001). A prompt that reminds the model to try varied combinations gave no gain (average inventory 43, t=-1.17, p=0.304).
limits: Interventions on SAE features were limited to the model family tested.
agent_relevance: Telling a model to explore does not fix it. Add structure that forces a pause before choosing.

source: Damani et al. (2024) Learning How Hard to Think: Input-Adaptive Allocation of LM Computation
finding: A learned difficulty predictor allocates best-of-k samples per query. Same quality with far less compute on code and math.
numbers: Math and Code: same performance with up to 50% less compute. Chat: 0-10% (full variant), 25-40% (tranches variant). Routing: call the costly decoder only 50-75% of the time. Difficulty predictor accuracy 72-84%. Gains are marginal below budget 8.
limits: On code about 50% of problems have zero success rate, so a predicted 1% looks like a good bet for a large budget; the offline variant avoids this.
agent_relevance: Direct empirical support for G12: spend by predicted difficulty, and do not pour budget into hopeless items.

source: Snell et al. (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
finding: Per-prompt compute-optimal allocation (by difficulty bin) beat best-of-N with about 4x less compute. Best test-time method depends on difficulty.
numbers: More than 4x efficiency over best-of-N baseline. FLOPs-matched: on problems where the small model has non-trivial success, test-time compute beat a 14x larger model. On the hardest MATH level 5, no method made meaningful progress. Beam search worse than best-of-N on levels 1-2, better on levels 3-4.
limits: PaLM 2-S* on MATH; difficulty is oracle or model-estimated bin.
agent_relevance: Source of G12. Easy: sample or revise; mid: search; hardest: do not search, give up or escalate.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
finding: Coverage (fraction solved by any sample) rises log-linearly with sample count over four orders of magnitude. It helps most when a verifier exists.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite: 15.9% with 1 sample to 56% with 250, above single-attempt SOTA 43%. CodeContests, Gemma-2B: 0.02% at 1 sample to 7.1% at 10,000. MATH Llama-3-8B: 82.9% at 100 samples to 98.44% at 10,000, but majority vote or reward model gained only 40.50% to 41.41%.
limits: Fixed budget per problem, not adaptive.
agent_relevance: Qualifies the foothold rule: with a cheap verifier, even tiny success rates can be mined by huge sampling. Without one, extra samples do not convert to answers.

source: Aggarwal et al. (2023) Let's Sample Step by Step: Adaptive-Consistency
finding: A Dirichlet-based stopping rule halts majority-vote sampling once the lead is safe. A sequential-test cousin of bandit allocation.
numbers: 17 datasets, 3 LLMs: up to 7.9x fewer samples with average accuracy drop under 0.1%. Example: 4x savings at 0.04% drop.
limits: Stops on agreement; cannot detect consistently wrong answers.
agent_relevance: Cheap stop rule for repeated attempts; compare with a fixed two-agree rule.

source: Li et al. (2024) Escape Sky-high Cost: Early-Stopping Self-Consistency (ESC)
finding: Sample in small windows and stop when a window is unanimous. Cuts samples with comparable accuracy.
numbers: Average sample cut: MATH -33.8%, GSM8K -80.1%, StrategyQA -76.8%, CommonsenseQA -78.5%, Coin Flip -84.2%, Last Letters -67.4%.
limits: Savings depend on how often the task has unanimous easy items.
agent_relevance: Same message: easy items need few samples. Hard items keep the budget.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Language Agent Tree Search (LATS)
finding: An LLM agent loop that runs Monte Carlo tree search with UCT selection over actions, with LM value estimates and reflections.
numbers: HumanEval Pass@1: GPT-4 92.7; GPT-3.5 LATS 83.8 vs Reflexion 68.1, CoT 46.9. Average +22.1 on WebShop with GPT-3.5.
limits: Costs more LLM calls than ReAct; UCT constant is a tuned weight; gains rely on environment feedback or tests.
agent_relevance: A bandit rule (UCT) already living inside an LLM agent loop. Check cost per solved problem before adopting.

source: Li et al. (2024) Efficient Prompt Optimization Through the Lens of Best Arm Identification (TRIPLE)
finding: Treats choosing a prompt from a pool as fixed-budget best-arm identification and uses sequential halving and continuously-reject.
numbers: Budget 150: TRIPLE-SH and TRIPLE-CR beat Uniform by 15% and 12% (GPT-3.5), 15% and 16% (Llama2); beat UCB by 5% and 3% (GPT-3.5), 6% and 7% (Llama2). Embedding variants beat BO-EI and NeuralUCB by 10-56%.
limits: Gains are relative accuracy on instruction-induction style tasks.
agent_relevance: Sequential halving is a ready rule for spending an evaluation budget over candidate ideas.

source: Lee et al. (2023) Supervised Pretraining Can Learn In-Context RL (DPT)
finding: A transformer trained to predict the optimal action from a context of past interactions behaves like posterior (Thompson) sampling and explores online on bandits, with regret guarantees.
numbers: Trained on 5-armed bandits; compared against empirical mean, UCB, Thompson sampling and LCB. No exact figures recorded.
limits: Small purpose-trained transformer, not a language model.
agent_relevance: Exploration can be learnt, but needs weight training; not usable by a scaffold alone.

source: Laskin et al. (2022) In-Context RL with Algorithm Distillation
finding: A transformer trained on UCB learning histories explores bandit arms in context and learns a more data-efficient policy than the source algorithm.
numbers: 10-arm adversarial bandit, 100 trials; scores normalised to UCB; also Dark Room and Watermaze. No exact figures recorded.
limits: Needs a training run; not an LLM prompt method.
agent_relevance: Algorithm distillation is the training analogue of what the EVOLvE guide does at inference.

source: Park et al. (2024/2025) Do LLM Agents Have Regret?
finding: LLM agents reach sublinear regret in many adversarial online learning and repeated-game settings, but GPT-4 fails to be no-regret in simple cases.
numbers: Trend-checking test of regret growth; proposes a regret-loss for training with guarantees for single-layer self-attention. No exact figures recorded.
limits: Adversarial (non-stochastic) setting, not the stochastic bandit of Gittins.
agent_relevance: No-regret failures in simple cases mean an agent should not rely on in-context learning for allocation alone.

source: Gittins (1979) Bandit processes and dynamic allocation indices; Gittins, Glazebrook & Weber (2011) Multi-armed Bandit Allocation Indices
finding: Gittins index: for discounted, independent arms the optimal rule is to play the arm with the highest index. Not read this session; stated from memory.
numbers: Not read; no numbers recorded.
limits: Needs independent arms, geometric discounting, one arm at a time. Index is costly to compute, so LLM work uses UCB or Thompson as stand-ins.
agent_relevance: Theory root for G12. Use only through simpler rules unless the arms are well modelled.

source: Wilson et al. (2014) Humans use directed and random exploration to solve the explore-exploit dilemma
finding: Original horizon task: more free choices left leads humans to pick the less-known option more (directed) and to choose more noisily (random). Not read; known only as described in Binz & Schulz.
numbers: Four forced trials, then 1 or 6 free trials, per Binz & Schulz description.
limits: Not opened this session.
agent_relevance: The paradigm used to test LLMs in c09 and in Pan et al.
